If there are any syntax errors (e.g., missing braces, stray commas, incorrect import paths), the page will fail to load and I’ll waste time debugging runtime errors that could have been caught earlier.

I already confirmed that the required libraries (three.module.js and OrbitControls.js) are present and look correct (the header shows the license comment and an `import` statement). I also verified that the texture JPEG files have proper magic bytes, so the assets themselves seem fine. The next logical step is to run a static syntax check on the newly created main.js.

Node.js is installed on the system (the earlier PowerShell check returned `C:\Program Files (x86)\nodejs\node.exe`). Node can perform an ES‑module syntax check using the `--check` flag, but it expects a file with an `.mjs` extension or a package.json specifying `"type": "module"`. To avoid modifying the project structure, I’ll copy main.js to a temporary location, rename it with a `.mjs` extension, and then invoke `node --check` on that temporary file. If the check passes, Node will exit with status 0; I’ll then echo a marker string (`SYNTAX_OK`) so I can easily detect success in the tool output.

Using PowerShell lets me chain these commands cleanly: first `Copy-Item` to place the file in `$env:TEMP\main_check.mjs` (overwriting any previous copy), then `node --check $env:TEMP\main_check.mjs`, and finally `echo SYNTAX_OK`. This single command will either produce an error message from Node (if there’s a syntax problem) or output `SYNTAX_OK` (if everything is fine). Running it now will give me confidence before proceeding to launch a server or open the HTML page.

Thus, the appropriate next action is to issue this PowerShell command.
